newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan central bank bullish for 1997 economy.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan central bank bullish for 1997 economy.

text.p: Taiwan's central bank showed general optimism about the island's economic outlook for 1997 on Tuesday and vowed to maintain a loose monetary policy to ensure healthy economic growth.

The central bank, in a year-end package of projections for the coming year, said it expected the island's gross domestic product to grow 6.17 percent in 1997, up from an official forecast of 5.7 percent for 1996.
It said that consumer prices could be expected to rise by 3.31 percent in 1997 and that wholesale prices should fall 0.23 percent, continuing their recent downward trend.

"A stable recovery of global economy and an expansion of world trade will further widen the nation's exports, imports and trade deficit," bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong told reporters at a year-end news conference.
"The economy will gradually recover next year and demand for liquidity will increase," Sheu said. "The (economy) is expected to show a better performance than this year."
In trade, the central bank projected that Taiwan could expect 1997 exports to grow 8.39 percent, up from an official 1996 full-year forecast of 6.8 percent.
The island's imports were expected to grow 7.34 percent in 1997, up from 1996's forecast of 4.11 percent, the central bank said in an official statement.

Sheu said the government's determination to remove investment barriers would greatly boost investment willingness in the private sector, adding that private investment was likely to rise 8.5 percent in 1997.
Citing expectations of economic recovery and growing liquidity demand in 1997, the bank would maintain its stable-to-loose monetary policy and not lower its money-supply growth targets.
"The priority is to maintain the stability of consumer prices and finance. We will continue in future to execute our stable-to-loose monetary policy," Sheu said.

Sheu said the bank's target for growth of the broadest measure of money supply, M2, would not be lowered from its 9 to 14 percent level, despite a top state economic planner saying that a reduction to between 8 and 13 percent had been agreed.
"The main reason that M2 growth did not meet the target zone was that the economic recovery has not been as fast as projected and (therefore) demand for liquidity was weak," Sheu said.
The central bank and other agencies have said a modest recovery begun in the fourth quarter of 1996 would pick up steam in 1997.

The governor did not stray from the central bank's position, stated repeatedly in recent months, that monetary policy should be kept where it was to ensure adequate financing for any recovery without fuelling inflation or undermining citizens' deposits.

Sheu said the central bank's policy in principle was to gradually reduce banks' reserve requirements so as to ensure adequate liquidity in the market, but made clear that it had no plans to do so now.

The bank has reduced banks' reserve requirements five times since mid-1995 and the lack of a significant impact on Taiwan's hoped-for recovery has sobered the central bank governor about their effectiveness.
Sheu has said often that reserve requirement adjustments were no cure-all for an ailing economy.
